title: OCC Bulletin 2026-54: Examiner Framework for Agentic AI in Banking
excerpt: OCC Bulletin 2026-54: Examiner Framework for Agentic AI in Banking. Authors: Cloud Security Alliance AI Safety Initiative Published: 2026-11-13 Categories: AI Governance and Regulation. Download PDF Download Markdown. OCC Bulletin 2026-54: Examiner Framework for Agentic AI in Banking. Key Takeaways. On November 4, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued Bulletin 2026-54, “Super Intelligence: Supervisory Framework,” together with a framework document that tells national bank examiners how to evaluate banks’ use of generative and agentic AI [1][2][3]. “Super Intelligence” (SI) is the OCC’s term for the technologies previously called “artificial intelligence,” a change in wording that follows Executive Order 14434 [1][5]. It is not a claim about the capability of the systems under review. The framework is the OCC’s first dedicated examiner resource to address agentic systems directly. It fills the gap left in April 2026, when the revised interagency model risk management guidance (OCC Bulletin 2026-13) placed generative and agentic AI outside its scope [2][4]. The first point for security, risk, and vendor teams is that the framework is an examiner tool, not a rule. The OCC says it “does not establish supervisory expectations for banks,” but in practice it shows what examiners will ask about [1]. The second is that consequences matter more than sophistication. Control intensity scales with the decision consequence, reversibility, impact, autonomy, data sensitivity, explainability, and provenance of each use case, so an autonomous customer-facing payment agent sits at Tier 1 “regardless of how well it performs in testing” [2]. Third, agentic failure counts as a resilience event: the framework expects banks to detect and contain an agent that “could remain available while taking inappropriate or harmful actions,” using tools such as circuit breakers, rate limits, least privilege, and kill switches [2]. Two further points concern identity and vendors. Agents should be governed as non-human identities, since the framework says agent credentials and permissions may be governed “in a manner comparable to privileged users” and treats the breadth of an agent’s tool access as attack surface [2]. Vendor relationships also face closer scrutiny. Examiners will look at the scope of provider agents’ authority, SI incident definitions, liability allocation, and notice when vendors add SI features to products a bank already uses [2]. Background. From SR 11-7 to a Gap for Generative and Agentic AI. For fifteen years, bank oversight of quantitative models in the United States rested on OCC Bulletin 2011-12 and the parallel Federal Reserve SR 11-7. Supervisors and banks also stretched that guidance to cover machine learning. On April 17, 2026, the OCC, Federal Reserve, and FDIC replaced it with shorter, risk-based guidance issued as OCC Bulletin 2026-13, SR 26-2, and FIL-15-2026 [4][7]. The revised guidance narrowed what counts as a “model,” stated that it does not create enforceable standards, and left generative and agentic AI out of scope [4][7]. Bulletin 2026-54 now confirms the division of labor in a footnote. The principles of Bulletin 2026-13 apply to non-generative, non-agentic SI models, so the new framework “is more applicable to generative and agentic SI” [2]. The vocabulary comes from Executive Order 14434, “Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence,” published at 91 Fed. Reg. 63129 on October 2, 2026. The order directs federal agencies to use “Super Intelligence” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” [5]. The OCC defines SI as the technologies previously covered by the statutory definition of AI in 15 U. S. C. 9401(3), “as well as the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of those technologies” [2]. title: Inside Banco BAI’s Core Banking Migration and Its Plan for Responsible AI
excerpt: When someone transfers money, checks an account balance or makes a payment, they rarely think about the banking technology making those services possible. Yet every transaction depends on banking systems that manage financial records and allow customers to access their money. Upgrading that technology can be especially challenging when a bank must continue serving millions of customers throughout the process. Banco Angolano de Investimentos (Banco BAI), one of Angola's leading financial institutions, is preparing for a major core banking migration currently planned for 2027. The project will move customer accounts, banking products, loan portfolios and transaction histories to a newer platform designed to support faster payments and more connected digital services. The bank also plans to expand its use of generative AI, building on Luena 2. 0, its existing virtual assistant. Founded in 1996 and headquartered in Luanda, Banco BAI serves approximately 3 million customers and is celebrating its 30th anniversary in 2026. The BAI Group also operates in Portugal through BAI Europa, Cape Verde through BAI Cabo Verde and São Tomé and Príncipe through BISTP. It was the first Angolan institution to receive credit ratings from both Fitch (B-, Stable) and Moody's (B3, Stable). As it looks toward the next decade, Banco BAI remains focused on improving its technology and introducing new services while preparing its systems and internal processes to support those changes without disrupting customers. Why Now? Banco BAI Targets 2027 for Its Core Banking Migration. Modern core banking platforms are now more flexible and better suited for cloud-based operations than they were a few years ago. Banco BAI plans to adopt a cloud-ready, API-first platform that will make it easier for different banking systems to share information and introduce new services without the limitations of older technology. Banco BAI has also strengthened its internal capabilities in regulatory compliance, data governance and change management, preparing the institution for a migration that will affect nearly every part of its operations. "A core banking migration is one of the largest, highest-risk transformations a bank can undertake,” Banco BAI explained. “It touches every account, every product, every channel and every reporting line. ”. Banco BAI also plans to update internal workflows and retrain employees to use the new systems. To help minimize service disruptions, the migration is expected to include an extended parallel-run period, during which the existing and new systems will operate simultaneously before the transition is completed. International banking standards have also influenced the timing. Banks are increasingly adopting ISO 20022, which provides a consistent way for financial institutions to exchange payment information. Banco BAI believes further delays could make it harder to keep pace with these changes. “The timing is deliberate,” the bank explained. What Banco BAI Hopes to Achieve With Its New Core Banking System. Beyond replacing older infrastructure, Banco BAI's planned migration is intended to support banking capabilities that are difficult or impossible to offer through its existing systems. One priority is real-time processing, which would allow transactions and account information to be updated immediately rather than waiting for scheduled processing. The bank also aims to support instant payments on a larger scale, allowing it to handle higher volumes of payment activity. Another planned capability is open banking, which would allow authorized third-party applications to connect with Banco BAI's systems through defined interfaces. This could make it easier to offer financial services that work across different platforms. The new system is also expected to include compliance checks directly within transaction processing, allowing the bank to review activity against regulatory requirements as transactions are handled. title: Gen Z Warms to AI Banking Tools
excerpt: . Gen Z Warms to AI Banking Tools. A survey of bank customers across eleven European countries finds younger adults are more receptive to AI-powered banking solutions than older customers. Updated on Nov. 10, 2026 in Banking. Live Poll. Would you be comfortable letting an AI chatbot handle talks about your debt?. The EOS Banking AI Barometer, a representative online survey of 4,400 bank customers aged 18 to 65 in eleven European countries, was conducted in July 2026. Results show Gen Z and millennials are more open to AI-powered bank solutions than older customers. Why it matters. Younger customers are more likely than the general population to report payment difficulties, making AI-driven banking support a potentially significant channel for financial assistance. The findings point to a widening generational gap in how customers want to interact with their banks. Among 18-34 year olds, 60% value AI for round-the-clock availability and 28% already use bank AI chatbots, compared with 47% and 13% of 51-65 year olds. The survey does not show whether these preferences translate into better outcomes for customers facing financial strain. The players. EOS Banking AI Barometer. A survey tracking European bank customers' attitudes toward artificial intelligence in banking services across eleven countries. The details. Respondents were asked about their attitudes toward AI in banking interactions, including speed, availability, and financial oversight. Only 14% of 18-34 year olds and 17% of 18-24 year olds said they would prefer to speak exclusively with AI about debt. Timeline. July 2026: EOS Banking AI Barometer survey conducted. November 10, 2026: Results published in a press release from Hamburg, Germany. Market Dynamics. The survey's age split suggests banks deploying AI chatbots are reaching their youngest customers first, while older customers remain more hesitant. Because the sample covers eleven European countries, the results offer a multinational view of how customer attitudes toward AI-driven banking are forming. Customers who use bank AI chatbots for everyday questions may see faster responses, but the survey does not indicate how these tools affect fees or account options. Anyone facing payment difficulties should compare how their bank's AI tools handle debt conversations with access to a human adviser. The takeaway. Customers comfortable with AI banking tools should still confirm that human support is available when debt or payment problems arise. Checking how a bank routes complex financial questions can help avoid relying on automated answers alone. Further reading.
